description: I’m Praise, a Calgary high schooler into robotics and game design. I’m building a Mars survival game for kids 7-12: run a base, balance power, shields and a greenhouse, and survive 10 sols until the supply rocket lands. Storms are based on NASA’s real May 2024 solar storm, with Curiosity rover facts after each one. Concept and NASA data ready. Looking for coders (JavaScript/Unity), artists and storytellers.
summary: Mars on Your Own is a Scratch game for kids aged 7 to 12. The base AI, ARIA, shuts down, and the player becomes Mission Control for a young crew on Mars. Kids keep three needs alive (radiation shield, muscles and food) for 90 seconds until ARIA reboots. When a real solar storm hits, based on NASA's May 2024 storm, kids learn a calm routine: Freeze, Spot, Fix. They have only one repair kit, so every fix is a trade-off: fix the shield, fix the exercise bike, or a clever fix that uses the water tank as radiation shielding but costs food. Crewmates cause problems too: a panicking sister and a friend who takes extra food and refuses to listen. Kids learn that people problems matter as much as broken machines. A message from the Curiosity rover shares the real radiation measured during the storm. We built it because kids are learning that AI is the first answer to everything. On Mars, help is minutes away, so they need to think for themselves.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: Mars on Your Own is a 2-minute Scratch game for kids 7-12. The player is Mission Control. The base AI, ARIA, goes offline, and Nova's crew must survive 90 seconds until it reboots. Kids click the exercise bike (muscles) and greenhouse (food) and protect the radiation shield. Halfway through, a solar storm hits. Kids follow Freeze (pause and breathe), Spot (click what broke) and Fix (one repair kit, three choices, each with a cost). Crewmates cause human problems: Mia panics, Leo takes extra food and later refuses to listen ('ARIA was the boss!'). Kids must talk to them. A '2 weeks later' ending explains the real effects of radiation, exercise and food, and shows a base health score and how many crew problems were solved.

WHY IT MATTERS: The challenge asks for real mission trade-offs that kids can feel. Every fix in our game costs something, and the clever water-tank fix teaches that water blocks radiation. It also teaches calm problem-solving without AI, because on Mars help from Earth is minutes away.

HOW WE BUILT IT: Scratch 3 (so kids 7-12 can open and remix it), packaged with the TurboWarp Packager so it plays in any browser without an account. Art, sounds and scripts were made with code, with AI assistance (see SI section). Tested by playing through every path.

WHAT'S NEXT: Playtest with kids 7-12, add dust storms and more crew problems, and make a free 15-minute classroom lesson.

AI USE: We used Claude (an AI assistant by Anthropic) to help write the Scratch scripts, draw the game art with code, and synthesize the sound effects, and to help organize our slides. The game idea, story, characters, Freeze-Spot-Fix routine and design choices are our team's.
